conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, not a test of your parenting. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and you can pause or skip anything you’d like. We’ll cover ten gentle questions about the past seven days, and I’ll ask them in everyday language. Ready to start?

In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?
I guess I can still laugh sometimes—like yesterday my husband made a silly joke and I chuckled—but most of the time it feels kind of forced. Humor just doesn’t come as easily as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes, yes, but it takes a lot more effort than before. I still laugh a little if something’s really funny, but the lightness fades fast and I’m right back to feeling flat.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I’ll plan a walk with a friend or picking up a coffee, and part of me hopes it’ll feel good, but when the time comes it’s kind of “meh.” I still go, and once in a while I’ll enjoy it for a few minutes, but it’s nowhere near the excitement I used to feel.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Like if the baby won’t settle, I automatically think I must be doing something wrong or that I’m just not a good mom. Even little things—spilling some pumped milk or being five minutes late to an appointment—turn into this loop of “I should’ve known better.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Most days, yeah. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s fine, nothing’s happening, but my chest feels tight and my mind keeps jumping to “what if he stops breathing?” or “what if I drop him?” I know it’s not logical, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week I’ve had that sudden rush—like my heart’s racing and I feel I can’t get a full breath. There’s no real danger, but the fear just spikes. I usually rock the baby’s bassinet with my foot while I try to breathe slow; it passes after a few minutes, but it’s unsettling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… a lot of the time. Some days it feels like the laundry, the dishes, the feedings, the texts I haven’t answered—everything—just piles up and I can’t see over it. I manage to get through what the baby needs, but the rest feels impossible.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries—about the baby, about tomorrow, about whether I’m doing any of this right. It takes me a long time to drift off, and when I do I wake up again with racing thoughts. It’s been like that most nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I still care for the baby and do what I have to, but there’s this constant ache in my chest and I catch myself tearing up for no clear reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes—twice this week. Once was when I couldn’t get him to latch, and I just sat there in the rocker with tears streaming down. The other time was after a phone call with my mom; she asked how I was doing and I said “fine,” but as soon as I hung up I started sobbing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of fleeting thoughts have popped into my head—like “what if I just didn’t wake up?”—but I’ve never pictured how I’d do it, and I don’t want to leave my baby. They’re more like exhausted, passing wishes that everything would stop for a minute, not an actual plan.

You've shared how the joy and spark that used to come easily now feel distant or forced: laughter fades quickly, planned outings feel flat, and an endless loop of self-blame whispers that you're failing as a mom. Most days bring a heavy, gray sadness, daily tears, and nights spent staring at the ceiling while anxious "what-ifs" race through your mind. Even simple tasks seem to pile up and suffocate you, and although you love your baby and don't want to die, you sometimes wish everything could just pause. These feelings are understandably frightening and exhausting, and they deserve prompt, compassionate attention.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in ability to laugh, needing extra effort and quick return to flat mood, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports markedly reduced enjoyment and anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, automatic self-blame for routine mishaps, aligning with 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries without cause, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic-like episodes multiple times in the week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and feeling buried under responsibilities despite meeting baby's needs</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing worries—matching "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with physical and emotional heaviness, constant ache, and frequent tearfulness—semantically matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two distinct crying episodes triggered by stressors, matching "Yes, quite often" (twice in a week).</sym>, <sym>Patient reports fleeting passive suicidal wishes ("didn't wake up") without intent or plan, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** This score places you well above the EPDS threshold (≥14) that flags probable major postpartum depression. You endorse core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, fatigue/loss of energy, insomnia, and recurrent thoughts of death. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (uncontrollable worry, episodic panic) are also prominent. Because of the intensity of symptoms, including passive suicidal ideation, you merit urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within the next few days
2. Arrange a follow-up mental-health assessment to develop a treatment plan (therapy, medication, or both)
3. Share these EPDS results and your safety status with a trusted partner, family member, or friend so you have support tonight
4. Create a brief safety plan: list 24/7 hotlines (<med>988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline</med>), local emergency numbers, and two people you can call if thoughts become more intense
5. Begin gentle sleep-hygiene steps: wind-down routine, dim lights, hand baby to partner/friend for one night feed if possible, and limit screens after feeds
6. Consider starting evidence-based psychotherapy such as <med>Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy</med> or <med>Interpersonal Therapy</med> tailored for postpartum depression
7. Discuss with your provider whether a short-term antidepressant (e.g., sertraline) is appropriate while breastfeeding
8. Reach out to local or online postpartum support groups for peer encouragement and practical coping ideas
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Note

Symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
- Marked guilt/self-blame over routine infant care  
- Generalized anxiety, intrusive worries about infant safety, two panic episodes this week  
- Sleep-onset insomnia linked to racing thoughts  
- Frequent feeling overwhelmed by ordinary tasks  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan, intent, or desire to die; states wish to “pause”)

Pattern  
Responses cluster in the moderate–severe range for depressive and anxiety symptoms, consistent with possible major postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety.

Risk flags  
- Daily sadness, crying, anhedonia  
- Self-blame/feelings of inadequacy  
- Anxiety attacks and chronic worry  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Passive SI present → safety concern (low imminent risk per pt report)

Screening impression  
High screening probability for postpartum major depressive episode with co-occurring anxiety; passive suicidal thoughts noted. Recommend comprehensive clinical evaluation and safety-planning follow-up.
